--- title: "Interactive Plots" author: "Sparrow" date: "2026-11-20" format: html: code-copy: true toc: true lightbox: auto execute: warning: false message: false --- A static figure is right for a paper. An **interactive** one helps when readers explore: hover for the exact value of one point, zoom into a busy period, switch groups on and off, or click a district on a map. Interactive figures work in **HTML** output (a Quarto web page, a dashboard, a Shiny app); in PDF or Word they are not available, so keep a static version for the paper. This page uses three packages, each an `htmlwidget` that Quarto embeds in the page: **plotly** (charts), **DT** (tables) and **leaflet** (maps), plus **crosstalk** to link them. Data: the NCD survey (`data/ncd_survey.csv`) and the district blocks of the GIS track. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) library(plotly) ncd <- read_csv(c("../data/ncd_survey.csv", "data/ncd_survey.csv")[file.exists(c("../data/ncd_survey.csv", "data/ncd_survey.csv"))][1], show_col_types = FALSE) |> mutate(phys_act = factor(phys_act, levels = c("low", "moderate", "high"))) ``` ::: ## 1. Any ggplot, made interactive: `ggplotly()` Build the plot as usual, then pass it to `ggplotly()`. The `text` aesthetic sets what the tooltip shows. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p <- ggplot(ncd, aes(age, sbp, colour = sex, text = paste0("id ", id, "
age ", age, "
SBP ", sbp, " mmHg
BMI ", bmi))) + geom_point(alpha = 0.6) + labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Systolic BP (mmHg)", colour = NULL) ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: - **Hover** a point to read its values; **drag** to zoom; **double-click** to reset. - **Click a legend entry** to hide that group, double-click to show it alone. - `tooltip = "text"` limits the tooltip to the text you wrote; the default lists every aesthetic. ## 2. Categories: bars and boxes with hover labels ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} by_act <- ncd |> group_by(phys_act) |> summarise(n = n(), pct = round(100 * mean(htn), 1)) p <- ggplot(by_act, aes(phys_act, pct, text = paste0(pct, "% of ", n, " people"))) + geom_col(fill = "#2C5F8D") + labs(x = "Physical activity", y = "Hypertension (%)") ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplotly(ggplot(ncd, aes(phys_act, sbp)) + geom_boxplot(fill = "grey85") + labs(x = "Physical activity", y = "Systolic BP (mmHg)")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: The box tooltip gives the **median, quartiles and fences** of each group: useful in a meeting, where nobody can read values off a static axis. ## 3. Native plotly: a histogram with a group switch `plot_ly()` builds charts directly. Here two overlaid histograms; click a legend entry to compare one sex at a time. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_ly(ncd, x = ~bmi, color = ~sex, type = "histogram", alpha = 0.6, nbinsx = 30) |> layout(barmode = "overlay", xaxis = list(title = "BMI (kg/m²)"), yaxis = list(title = "People")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## 4. Time: a line with a range slider ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dengue <- read_csv(c("../data/dengue_wards.csv", "data/dengue_wards.csv")[file.exists(c("../data/dengue_wards.csv", "data/dengue_wards.csv"))][1], show_col_types = FALSE) |> group_by(date) |> summarise(cases = sum(cases), rain_mm = mean(rain_mm)) plot_ly(dengue, x = ~date, y = ~cases, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", name = "Dengue cases") |> layout(xaxis = list(title = NULL, rangeslider = list(visible = TRUE)), yaxis = list(title = "Cases per month")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: Drag the ends of the slider to zoom into one season; the y-axis keeps its scale, so seasons stay comparable. ## 5. A searchable table: DT ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(DT) ncd |> select(id, village, age, sex, bmi, sbp, dbp, htn) |> datatable(rownames = FALSE, filter = "top", options = list(pageLength = 5)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: - `filter = "top"` adds a filter box above each column; sort by clicking a header. - Use it for **lists readers look things up in** (facilities, villages); not as a substitute for a summary table. ## 6. Linked views: crosstalk `crosstalk::SharedData` lets two widgets use **the same rows**: select points in the scatter plot and the table shows only those people. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(crosstalk) shared <- SharedData$new(ncd |> select(id, age, sex, sbp, dbp, bmi)) bscols(widths = c(6, 6), plot_ly(shared, x = ~dbp, y = ~sbp, type = "scatter", mode = "markers", alpha = 0.5) |> layout(xaxis = list(title = "Diastolic BP"), yaxis = list(title = "Systolic BP")) |> highlight(on = "plotly_selected", off = "plotly_deselect"), datatable(shared, rownames = FALSE, options = list(pageLength = 6, dom = "tp"))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: Choose the **box select** tool (top right of the plot), drag over the points with high systolic BP, and the table lists who they are. This works in a static HTML page: no server is needed. ## 7. Maps: leaflet ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(leaflet); library(sf) blocks <- st_read(c("../data/gis/district_blocks.geojson", "data/gis/district_blocks.geojson")[file.exists(c("../data/gis/district_blocks.geojson", "data/gis/district_blocks.geojson"))][1], quiet = TRUE) pal <- colorNumeric("YlOrRd", blocks$dengue_per_100k) leaflet(blocks) |> addProviderTiles(providers$CartoDB.Positron) |> addPolygons(fillColor = ~pal(dengue_per_100k), fillOpacity = 0.8, color = "white", weight = 1, label = ~block_name, popup = ~paste0("", block_name, "
Population: ", format(population, big.mark = ","), "
Dengue: ", dengue_per_100k, " per 100,000")) |> addLegend(pal = pal, values = ~dengue_per_100k, title = "Dengue per 100k") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: - Hover a block for its name; **click** it for the popup. - The base map tiles load from the internet; the shaded blocks do not need a connection. - Mapping rules (class breaks, rates rather than counts) are in the [GIS track](../gis/maps_choropleth.qmd). ## When to use interactivity | Use it when | Avoid it when | |---|---| | Readers explore many points or groups | The figure has one message: a static plot says it faster | | Exact values matter on hover | The output is PDF, Word or print | | Dashboards, teaching, data checking | Hiding information behind a hover that every reader needs | ::: callout-tip ## Checklist - Keep a **static version** for the paper; the interactive one goes in the supplement or a web appendix. - Write the **tooltip** yourself: units, rounding, the n. - Large data (more than about 50,000 points) makes the page slow: summarise first, or use `toWebGL()`. - Save a widget as its own file with `htmlwidgets::saveWidget(widget, "fig.html")`. - Other packages: **ggiraph** (interactive ggplot2 layers), **highcharter**, **echarts4r**; Shiny when a reader should change the analysis, not just the view. ::: ## Practise in R Download the lab **[Interactive plots](../labs/dataviz/v4_interactive.R)** and the data ([ncd_survey.csv](../data/ncd_survey.csv)). Fill in the blanks (`___`); the comments say what each step should do. ## Self-check quiz ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="ia1" data-type="mcq" data-hash="14ibmd.6md1tr" data-show="U2hvd3Mgb25seSB0aGUgdGV4dCBhZXN0aGV0aWMgb24gaG92ZXI=" data-explain="dG9vbHRpcCA9ICJ0ZXh0IiBsaW1pdHMgdGhlIGhvdmVyIGxhYmVsIHRvIHRoZSB0ZXh0IGFl c3RoZXRpYyB5b3UgYnVpbHQ7IHRoZSBkZWZhdWx0IGxpc3RzIGV2ZXJ5IG1hcHBlZCBhZXN0 aGV0aWMu"} In `ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text")`, what does the tooltip argument do? - Adds a text label beside each point - Shows only the text aesthetic on hover - Turns the axis titles into links - Exports the plot as a text file on disk ::: ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="ia2" data-type="mcq" data-hash="14iov2.6mdgb4" data-show="SXQgbmVlZHMgYSBzdGF0aWMgdmVyc2lvbiBmb3IgdGhlIFBERg==" data-explain="aHRtbHdpZGdldHMgd29yayBpbiBIVE1MIG9ubHk6IHB1dCBhIHN0YXRpYyBmaWd1cmUgaW4g dGhlIHBhcGVyIGFuZCB0aGUgaW50ZXJhY3RpdmUgb25lIGluIGEgd2ViIHN1cHBsZW1lbnQu "} Your paper goes to a journal as a PDF. What about the interactive plotly figure? - It is converted to an animation in the PDF - It needs a static version for the PDF - It works if the reader opens the PDF online - It is printed with all the tooltips shown ::: ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="ia3" data-type="mcq" data-hash="14j23s.6mdusi" data-show="TGluayB3aWRnZXRzIHNvIGEgc2VsZWN0aW9uIGZpbHRlcnMgdGhlIG90aGVycw==" data-explain="V2lkZ2V0cyBidWlsdCBvbiB0aGUgc2FtZSBTaGFyZWREYXRhIG9iamVjdCByZXNwb25kIHRv IGVhY2ggb3RoZXIncyBzZWxlY3Rpb25zLCBpbiBhIHN0YXRpYyBwYWdlIHdpdGhvdXQgYSBz ZXJ2ZXIu"} What does crosstalk's `SharedData` let you do? - Share a plot on social media from the page - Store the data on a server for other users - Link widgets so a selection filters the others - Speed up a plot by sharing memory between widgets ::: **Your score: ** (first attempt counts) ```{=html} ```
